name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 4 September 1971

clue.text: Coats not necessarily made of green stuff

definitions.text: Coats not necessarily made of green stuff

blocks.clueFragment: Coats not necessarily made of green stuff
blocks.note: surface reading: outer garments that need not be cut from green cloth
setter's reading: the coats are named after a green vegetable whose pod is its own jacket

explanation.surface: A tailor reassures a customer that these coats come in colours other than green.
explanation.walkthrough: A pea jacket is a short heavy woollen sailor's coat; the name has nothing to do with peas, which is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A pea jacket is a thick double-breasted reefer coat worn by sailors, so it is literally a kind of coat.

clue.text: Cast one's vote for such an all-rounder?

definitions.note: describes a person; the answer is the adjective for such a person

blocks.note: first meaning: to choose decisively, used with 'for'
second meaning: well rounded in figure, chubby

explanation.walkthrough: An all-rounder sounds like a versatile cricketer, but here it is someone round all over.
explanation.definitionFit: To plump for something is an idiom meaning to choose it firmly, and plump also describes a pleasantly fat, rounded body.

clue.text: Materials for building those imaginary castles?

definitions.text: Materials for building those imaginary castles?

blocks.clueFragment: Materials for building those imaginary castles?
blocks.note: surface reading: what daydreamers build their fantasies from
setter's reading: castles in the air, so bricks for the air; real perforated bricks used for ventilation

explanation.surface: A whimsical question about what one would use to build castles in the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: Daydreams are proverbially castles in the air; the real building item is a perforated brick that lets air through a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: Air bricks are genuine building materials, perforated blocks set into walls to provide ventilation under floors.

clue.text: A bit of a fight, the whole fight too - so things get rumoured

definitions.note: describes how rumours travel; the answer is an adverbial phrase

blocks.note: a round is one section of a boxing match
too means in addition
a bout is an entire boxing contest

explanation.surface: A boxing commentator links one round to the whole contest and the gossip that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Rumours spread here and there through a community, passing from person to person in every direction.

clue.text: " don't last: cookery do!" (Meredith)

blocks.note: surface reading: a quotation with its opening word missing
setter's reading: the gap is the word George Meredith wrote in The Ordeal of Richard Feverel, contrasting love with cooking

explanation.walkthrough: This is a fill-in-the-blank quotation: Meredith's line sets the passing pleasure of romance against the lasting value of good cooking.
explanation.definitionFit: Meredith's aphorism in The Ordeal of Richard Feverel opens with this word, meaning amorous embracing that soon fades.

clue.text: Neaera's locks in need of attention

definitions.text: Neaera's locks in need of attention

blocks.note: surface reading: the hair of Neaera, a nymph in Milton's Lycidas
setter's reading: Milton's phrase for her hair names knots that need combing out

explanation.surface: A classical nymph's hair badly needs brushing.
explanation.walkthrough: Milton's Lycidas speaks of playing with 'the tangles of Neaera's hair'; the clue adds that such hair needs attention.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton's poem uses this word for the knotted curls of Neaera's hair, and knotted hair is exactly what needs combing.

clue.text: She gets two numbers of the Arabian Nights!

blocks.clueFragment: two numbers of the Arabian Nights
blocks.note: the Arabian Nights are the Thousand and One Nights, and 1001 in Roman numerals is MI; two of those side by side

explanation.surface: A woman is granted a couple of tales from the Arabian Nights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Numbers' suggests songs or stories, but it means the figure 1001 written as Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: Mimi is a woman's name, most famously the heroine of Puccini's opera La Boheme.

clue.text: It seems to be not uninhabited in the main

definitions.note: a locative phrase standing for a thing found at sea, while the answer is a noun

blocks.note: it is, in the verb form
a let house has tenants, so it is not empty

explanation.surface: Something out at sea appears to have people living on it after all.
explanation.walkthrough: The main is an old word for the open sea, so the definition points to a small piece of land surrounded by ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: An islet is a tiny island, the kind of land that sits out in the open ocean.

clue.text: In rude surroundings five are unable to pay their way

definitions.text: are unable to pay their way
definitions.note: a verb phrase, while the answer is an adjective

indicators.note: in places one item inside the surroundings formed by another word

blocks.note: rude and insolent are synonyms
V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: Five people living in rough conditions cannot cover their costs.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone insolvent lacks the funds to meet their debts, so they cannot pay their way.

clue.text: Puffed with exercise and such a noisy bore!

blocks.note: pneumatic means filled with air, inflated
drill is military exercise

explanation.surface: Someone out of breath from a workout turns out to be a tiresome bore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bore' looks like a dull person, but it is a tool that bores holes.
explanation.definitionFit: A road-breaking machine powered by compressed air is famously loud and bores into concrete.

clue.text: Eradicates our post in a reshuffle

indicators.note: a reshuffle rearranges the order of things, as with a cabinet or a pack of cards

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cabinet reshuffle wipes out a minister's job.
explanation.definitionFit: To uproot something is to pull it out entirely, roots and all, which is what eradicate literally means.

clue.text: Puzzle-no more French?

blocks.note: French for no
French for more

explanation.surface: A puzzle that leaves the French speechless.
explanation.walkthrough: Non plus is French for 'no more', the state of being unable to go further, which is how the English verb arose.
explanation.definitionFit: To nonplus someone is to baffle or perplex them so completely they cannot respond.

clue.text: Long lasting belly noise, but without an inner turn

indicators.note: a turn swings the word round so it is read from the end back to the start
without in its old sense means outside, so one word wraps around the other

blocks.note: read as bell-y noise, the ringing of bells; probably a misprint for bell noise
taken as written

explanation.surface: A long rumble from the stomach, with a twist inside.
explanation.walkthrough: The ringing of bells is a peal; it goes outside the reversed word inner: PE-RENNI-AL.
explanation.definitionFit: Perennial means enduring year after year, so it describes anything long lasting.

clue.text: Some account I like to live up to

indicators.note: some means only part of the following words is used, a run of consecutive letters

blocks.note: found inside the string of these words

explanation.surface: A person describes a story they like and hope to live up to.
explanation.definitionFit: Until and up to are synonyms when marking a limit in time, as in waiting up to noon.

clue.text: Hadji's place

blocks.note: surface reading: the home of someone called Hadji
setter's reading: a hadji is a Muslim who has made the pilgrimage, so his place is its destination

explanation.walkthrough: A hadji is a Muslim who has completed the hajj, the pilgrimage to Islam's holiest city in Saudi Arabia.
explanation.definitionFit: The holy city in Saudi Arabia is where every hadji has travelled on pilgrimage, the goal of the hajj.

clue.text: For the dispatch of postal tuition courses?

definitions.text: For the dispatch of postal tuition courses?

blocks.note: surface reading: correspondence lessons, tutoring by post
setter's reading: a horse-drawn vehicle that carried letters, read as coaching by post

explanation.walkthrough: Coaching means tutoring, so coaching by post is a pun on the old horse-drawn vehicle that carried the post.
explanation.definitionFit: A mail coach was a stagecoach used to carry letters and parcels, so it was literally built for dispatching post.

clue.text: Light cloak?

blocks.note: surface reading: a cloak that weighs little
setter's reading: a lamp, whose glowing mesh hood is named after a cloak

explanation.walkthrough: Light seems to mean not heavy, but it is a lamp; a mantle is a cloak, and also the mesh hood that glows in a gas lamp.
explanation.definitionFit: A gas mantle is the incandescent mesh covering the flame of a gas lamp, and mantle is an old word for cloak.

clue.text: Beauty was the theme of Robert Bridges's

definitions.text: Beauty was the theme of Robert Bridges's

blocks.note: surface reading: a remark about a poet's favourite subject
setter's reading: the missing word completes the title of Bridges's long philosophical poem of 1929

explanation.walkthrough: Robert Bridges, Poet Laureate, wrote The Testament of Beauty; the clue's final word needs this title noun to complete it.
explanation.definitionFit: Bridges's long poem is titled The Testament of Beauty, so the word completes the possessive in the clue.

clue.text: I'd one suit to be turned

definitions.text: I'd one suit to be turned

indicators.note: turned means rearranged, flipped round so the order changes

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone wants a suit turned, the old thrift of remaking a worn suit with its unworn side outward.
explanation.definitionFit: A turned garment has been reversed so that its lining side shows, exactly what this phrase describes.

clue.text: "Ask where's the North? at York 'tis on the Tweed; in Scotland at the " (Pope)

definitions.text: "Ask where's the North? at York 'tis on the Tweed; in Scotland at the " (Pope)

blocks.clueFragment: "Ask where's the North? at York 'tis on the Tweed; in Scotland at the "
blocks.note: surface reading: a couplet with its last word missing
setter's reading: Pope's Essay on Man ends the line with the Latin name of the islands off Scotland's northern tip

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in quotation from Pope's Essay on Man: everyone thinks the North lies just beyond them, ending at the Orkney Islands.
explanation.definitionFit: Orcades is the Latin name for the Orkney Islands, the far northern archipelago off Scotland that Pope rhymed here.

clue.text: Cratchit Minimus, Peter . and I take a lot of beating

definitions.note: a verb phrase, while the answer is a plural noun

blocks.note: Tiny Tim is the youngest Cratchit in Dickens's A Christmas Carol; minimus is old school slang for the youngest of brothers
the name shortened to its initial, the full stop marking the abbreviation
an is an old form of and
taken as written

explanation.surface: The Cratchit boys from A Christmas Carol and the speaker get thrashed.
explanation.walkthrough: Minimus is the British public-school tag for the youngest of several brothers, and Tim is the youngest Cratchit.
explanation.definitionFit: Kettledrums are beaten with sticks throughout a performance, so they literally take a lot of beating.

clue.text: How those special supplements are presented

definitions.text: How those special supplements are presented

blocks.clueFragment: How those special supplements are presented
blocks.note: surface reading: the manner of publishing extra sections
setter's reading: split into two words, the answer describes the placing of loose pages within a magazine

explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words, the answer says how the pages arrive: placed in. As one word it is the extra leaf itself.
explanation.definitionFit: An inset is an extra page or section inserted into a newspaper or magazine, which is how supplements arrive.

clue.text: Small comfort for the peckish

blocks.note: surface reading: very little consolation
setter's reading: a tiny morsel of food for someone a little hungry

explanation.walkthrough: Peckish is British slang for slightly hungry; the phrase 'a small crumb of comfort' supplies the double edge.
explanation.definitionFit: A crumb is a tiny fragment of bread, scarcely enough to satisfy a mildly hungry person.

clue.text: If money talks, so do forgers

definitions.text: If money talks, so do forgers

blocks.note: surface reading: the proverb that wealth gets its way
setter's reading: forgers pass off fake money, and the legal verb for that also means to speak

explanation.walkthrough: In law, to pass counterfeit money is to utter it, so forgers 'talk' through the same verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Utter means to speak, and in legal language it also means to put forged notes or coins into circulation.

clue.text: Those engaged in dramatic errors?

blocks.note: surface reading: people making spectacular mistakes
setter's reading: actors performing Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors, or simply clowns making funny blunders on stage

explanation.walkthrough: Dramatic errors evokes Shakespeare's The Comedy of Errors, and performers in a comedy deliberately make errors for laughs.
explanation.definitionFit: Comic actors make deliberate blunders on stage for laughs, and Shakespeare's farce is called The Comedy of Errors.

clue.text: Places for viewers, say?

indicators.note: say asks for the word as spoken rather than as written

blocks.note: sights are things worth looking at for viewers

explanation.surface: A question about where spectators should go.
explanation.definitionFit: Sites are locations or plots of ground, so the word is a straightforward synonym for places.

clue.text: A maze with no gap

blocks.note: surface reading: a labyrinth
setter's reading: close the space between the two words to get a verb meaning to stun

explanation.walkthrough: Remove the space between 'A' and 'maze' and you get a verb meaning to astonish.
explanation.definitionFit: Amaze and astound are synonyms, both meaning to overwhelm someone with surprise.

clue.text: Fruit ingested by a worker for instance?

definitions.text: Fruit ingested by a worker for instance?

indicators.note: something ingested is swallowed, taken inside another body

blocks.note: a citrus fruit
a worker ant, the crossword's usual worker

explanation.surface: An insect eating a piece of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes food: fruit swallowed by an insect is an example of nourishment.
explanation.definitionFit: Aliment is a formal word for food or nourishment, and fruit eaten by anyone is an example of it.

clue.text: Swift runner sounds musical

indicators.note: sounds tells the solver to go by how a word is heard

blocks.note: Hair is the 1960s rock musical

explanation.surface: A fast athlete who also has a melodious voice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Musical' looks like an adjective but names the stage show Hair.
explanation.definitionFit: The animal is famous for its speed, as in the fable of the tortoise and the hare.

clue.text: So a cellist plays swing

indicators.note: plays suggests letters being toyed with and moved about freely

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cellist launches into a swing number.
explanation.definitionFit: To oscillate is to move to and fro regularly, like a pendulum, which is what swinging means.
